title: How each pauri sums up
hook: each pauri gathers the saloks before it into a stanza of its own

segments.voice: Yesterday, gaarab, pride, and your line: serve without argument. That closes a week: the thread of compassion, sootak, laaitbaaree, sweet speech, gaarab. Today, how the var holds them all together.
screen: `SERVE WITHOUT ARGUMENT.` · `A WEEK: THREADS, PURITY, SPEECH, SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Climb the steps down to the water at a gurdwara sarovar, or a staircase in an old Punjabi house, and every step has a name: pauri. The same word means a ladder rung. It's also the name of the stanzas you've been hearing for weeks without quite noticing them. Japji is built of pauris. So is every var in the Guru Granth Sahib. For three weeks we've mostly listened to saloks, the short verses about trees, threads and scales. Today, the steps they sit on.
screen: `A STEP DOWN TO THE WATER.` → `PAURI: A STEP, A RUNG.` → `THE STEPS UNDER THE SALOKS.`

segments.voice: A var, as we heard on day five hundred thirty-six, is an old Punjabi ballad form, sung about heroes and battles. Its stanzas are pauris, and in a var they march: each one a step forward in the story. The Guru Granth Sahib has twenty-two vars. In the Asa di Var, the pauris are Guru Nanak's, twenty-four of them, and they carry the main line of the poem: who the One is, how creation stands, what a true servant is like, what the Guru does. In front of each pauri sit two or more saloks, some Guru Nanak's, some Guru Angad's. Many scholars hold that they were set beside the pauris when Guru Arjan compiled the Granth, gathered by theme to open up the step that follows. So the saloks wander: a silk-cotton tree, a cartload of books, a thread, a kitchen. They make you see something. Then the pauri arrives and gathers what you've seen into one step forward. You've felt this already. The pauri where Guru Nanak says he's a sacrifice to the True Guru, who put wisdom on his eyes, came after saloks about show without substance. The saloks showed the problem; the pauri named the turning. Hear the Asa di Var sung and you can feel the rhythm: wander, gather; wander, gather. Many small pictures, then one step up. It's a way of learning that doesn't rush. You don't climb the whole staircase at once. You take the next pauri.
screen: `A VAR: A BALLAD OF HEROES.` · `24 PAURIS, GURU NANAK'S.` · `SALOKS WANDER, THE PAURI GATHERS.` · `WANDER, GATHER; ONE STEP UP.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: If you have a gutka or an app with the Asa di Var, read one pauri slowly, all the way through, in Gurmukhi or in translation. If not, hold the pauri from this week in mind: the contented ones served, did good, ate little, broke the world's chains, and the One kept giving more; let it sit as one step, complete, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end.
Pauri. A step, a ladder rung, and a stanza. In the Asa di Var, each of Guru Nanak's twenty-four pauris gathers the saloks before it into one step forward.
Your line: step by step. Nobody climbs a whole staircase in one stride. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: When Asa di Var is sung at dawn, ragis sing the saloks and then each pauri, and many Sikhs read the var from a gutka, pauri by pauri.

chat.says: Why does the Asa di Var keep switching between saloks and pauris?
options: The saloks wander and make you see; then Guru Nanak's pauri gathers it into one step forward.
The pauris are just short breaks for the singers, and the saloks carry the real message.
The saloks tell the story in order, and the pauris repeat it for anyone who missed it.
chat.meaning: In the Asa di Var, the saloks before each pauri open up a picture; Guru Nanak's pauri then gathers it into one step forward.
